story_type: giant cargo jet on wheels lands and takes off on a packed snow runway in Antarctica
hook: A loaded C-17 on wheels, landing on packed snow in Antarctica.
narration: A fully loaded C-17, on wheels, landing on a runway made of snow.
No wheeled, fully loaded cargo jet had ever landed and taken off on compacted snow before.
Army engineers spent more than sixteen months building this strip in Antarctica. They named it Phoenix Airfield.
Rollers weighing up to one hundred sixty thousand pounds packed the snow thirty two inches deep, hard enough to take the impact of a landing C-17.
On November fifteenth, two thousand sixteen, the jet came down and threw a wall of snow behind it.
Then it turned around, still loaded, and lifted off the same snow.
outcome: The Air Mobility Command certified the Phoenix runway in the field for heavy wheeled aircraft.
title: C-17 on wheels lands on Antarctic snow
description:
A McChord C-17 Globemaster III crew makes the first landing and takeoff of a wheeled, fully loaded cargo jet on the compacted snow runway at Phoenix Airfield, Antarctica, on Nov. 15, 2016.

Footage: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Engineer Research and Development Center, via DVIDS: https://www.dvidshub.net/video/596960/fully-loaded-c-17-uses-compacted-deep-snow-airfield-built-corps-engineers-rd

question_comment: Would you trust a runway made of snow under a 400,000 pound jet?

facts.claim: First landing and takeoff of a wheeled, fully loaded cargo jet on compacted snow
facts.source_quote: A McChord Air Force Base C-17 Globemaster III crew and the Army Corps of Engineers teamed up to make the first landing and takeoff of a wheeled and fully-loaded cargo aircraft on a compacted-snow runway
“This novel runway design and construction took more than 16 continuous months to complete,” said Terry Melendy, a CRREL research civil engineer.

facts.claim: 160,000 pound rollers, 32 inches deep, withstands a C-17 landing
facts.source_quote: The runway was designed using a compaction technique to modify the deep snow using heavy rollers weighing up to 160,000 pounds, to change the snow’s strength properties from its natural state creating a denser, higher strength snow foundation (32 inches deep) that can withstand the impact of a C-17 landing.

facts.claim: Certified in the field by Air Mobility Command
facts.source_quote: “The runway was certified in the field for heavy, wheeled aircraft by the Air Mobility Command,” said Melendy.
